units.title: Foundations
units.subtitle: Ein Sof, tzimtzum, the sefirot, and repair

lessons.title: Ein Sof: Without end
lessons.check_note: Etz Chaim 1:1 (Community Translation) and Tikkunei Zohar 17a (Solomon 2024) read on Sefaria 11/13. Scholem card from memory: check.

cards.title: Beyond every name
cards.body: **Kabbalah**, Jewish mysticism, starts with a God beyond anything we can picture or name. Kabbalists call this **Ein Sof**: without end.

cards.q: In Kabbalah, Ein Sof can be fully understood through careful thought.
cards.why: Etz Chaim: Ein Sof cannot be grasped "neither by thought nor by reflection."

cards.title: Without end
cards.body: Isaac Luria's teaching, as written down in **Etz Chaim**, begins with the highest light, **Ein Sof**: "it cannot be grasped in any way, neither by thought nor by reflection." It has **no beginning and no end**, and comes before everything that was ever created.

cards.title: One, but not in number
cards.body: A famous kabbalistic prayer opens with Elijah speaking: **Master of the Worlds**, You are One, but not one the way a number is one. You are high above all, hidden beyond all that is hidden: "no thought apprehends You at all."

cards.q: In Tikkunei Zohar 17a, what can no thought do?
cards.why: God is **beyond thought**: One, but not a number among numbers.

cards.gloss: "Whose presence fills all the earth!" (6:3). Etz Chaim says the same of the light of Ein Sof: before creation, it **filled all of existence**.

cards.title: Where Kabbalah comes from
cards.body: The **Zohar** presents itself as the teachings of **Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai** and his companions (2nd century). The scholar **Gershom Scholem** argued it was written in 13th-century **Spain**, largely by **Moses de León**. Three centuries later, **Isaac Luria** taught in Safed; his student **Chaim Vital** recorded his teaching in **Etz Chaim**.

src.ref: Gershom Scholem, Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism (1941)
src.note: from memory, not on Sefaria; check

cards.q: Which scholar argued that the Zohar was written in 13th-century Spain?
cards.why: **Scholem**, the founder of the modern study of Kabbalah.
wrong_why: Rashi lived before the Zohar appeared.
Maimonides died before the Zohar appeared.

src.ref: Gershom Scholem, Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism (1941)
src.note: from memory, not on Sefaria; check

cards.title: A God beyond pictures
cards.body: Your rabbi reads the Torah as a people **growing up**: from a child's picture of God as a hero, toward a God found in our choices. Kabbalah's **Ein Sof** pushes the same way: every picture of God is too small, so the old pictures have to be let go.

src.ref: Teaching from Jamie's rabbi (oral, as Jamie retold it); Etz Chaim 1:1
src.note: connection to Kabbalah is mine; check with Jamie

cards.prompt: Ein Sof is beyond every name and picture. Which picture of God from childhood have you outgrown, and what, if anything, took its place?

points: **Ein Sof**: without end, beyond thought (Etz Chaim).
Ein Sof's light **filled all of existence**.
Zohar: attributed to Shimon bar Yochai; Scholem: **13th-century Spain**.

lessons.title: Tzimtzum: Making room
lessons.check_note: Etz Chaim 1:2 (Community Translation) read on Sefaria 11/13.

cards.title: Where is there room?
cards.body: If God's light fills everything, where is there room for **a world**? Isaac Luria's answer is one of Kabbalah's boldest ideas.

cards.q: In Luria's teaching, what did Ein Sof do first to make room for the worlds?
choices: Contracted itself, leaving an empty space

cards.title: A light that filled everything
cards.body: Before anything was created, "there was a simple supernal light that filled all of existence." There was **no empty space** at all: only one equal light without beginning or end, the light of Ein Sof.

cards.title: Contraction
cards.body: When God willed to create, God **contracted** at the center point. The light withdrew to the sides, and an **empty space** was left, perfectly round, equal on every side. Kabbalists call this **tzimtzum**.

choices: God's contraction, leaving room for creation
cards.why: God **withdraws**, so something else can be.

cards.title: A line of light
cards.body: Into the empty space, a single **straight line** of light reaches down from Ein Sof, "like a thin tube." Through it, light reaches the worlds. It cannot pour in from every side: then everything would melt back into **the light of Ein Sof**, as it was at first.

cards.q: In Etz Chaim, why does light enter the empty space by one thin line, not from every side?
choices: Otherwise the worlds would dissolve back into Ein Sof
Light can only travel in lines
cards.why: Too much light, and **there would be no world**.

cards.title: Why create at all?
cards.body: Etz Chaim gives a reason: God wanted to be known as **merciful and gracious**. But if no one exists to receive mercy, "how can He be called merciful?" Creation makes room for **someone to receive kindness**.

cards.q: According to Etz Chaim, why did God create the worlds?
choices: So there would be someone to receive God's mercy

cards.prompt: Tzimtzum is God stepping back so that something else can exist. Where might you need to step back to make room for someone?

points: A thin **line of light** reaches the worlds.
Why? So **mercy** has someone to receive it.

lessons.title: The ten sefirot
lessons.check_note: Sefer Yetzirah 1:4, Pardes Rimonim 1:1 (Community Translation), Tikkunei Zohar 17a, Etz Chaim 1:2 read on Sefaria 11/13. Full list of ten names from memory: check.

cards.title: How the hidden is known
cards.body: If Ein Sof is beyond all thought, how is God known at all? Kabbalah answers: through **ten sefirot**, ten ways God's light reaches the world.

cards.q: Sefer Yetzirah insists there are exactly ten sefirot.
cards.why: "Ten and not nine, ten and not eleven."

cards.title: Ten and not nine
cards.body: The ancient **Sefer Yetzirah**, the Book of Formation, says: "Ten and not nine, ten and not eleven." Centuries later **Moses Cordovero** writes that all who study this wisdom agree the number is **ten**, and notes that Sefer Yetzirah is traditionally attributed to **Abraham**.

src.ref: Sefer Yetzirah 1:4; Pardes Rimonim 1:1 (Sefaria Community Translation)

cards.title: Constructs to direct worlds
cards.body: In the prayer of Elijah: You produced ten constructs, which we call **the ten sefirot**, to guide hidden worlds and revealed ones. You **bind and unite** them, and because You are within them, whoever separates one from another is as though they separated **You**.

cards.q: In Tikkunei Zohar 17a, why must the ten sefirot not be separated?
choices: God is within them, so splitting them splits God's unity

cards.gloss: "greatness, might, splendor, triumph, and majesty" (29:11). Kabbalists use these words as names of sefirot; Etz Chaim names **Gevurah, Tiferet, Netzach and Hod**.

cards.body: These are the words of **L'cha Adonai**, sung as the Torah is carried back to the Ark.

cards.title: The ten
cards.body: The usual list, from top to bottom: **Keter** (crown), **Chochmah** (wisdom), **Binah** (understanding), **Chesed** (kindness), **Gevurah** (strength), **Tiferet** (beauty), **Netzach** (endurance), **Hod** (splendor), **Yesod** (foundation), **Malchut** (kingship, also called **Shechinah**). Etz Chaim shows them in **three lines**, right, left and center.

src.ref: Standard kabbalistic list; Gershom Scholem, Kabbalah (1974); Etz Chaim 1:2 for the three lines
src.note: from memory, not on Sefaria; check

cards.q: Which verse, sung at the Torah service, gives several sefirot their names?

cards.prompt: Tikkunei Zohar warns against separating the sefirot, like kindness from strength. Which two of your own qualities do you find hardest to hold together?

points: "**Ten and not nine**, ten and not eleven" (Sefer Yetzirah).
Names from **1 Chronicles 29:11**: sung in L'cha Adonai.

lessons.title: Shechinah, broken vessels, and repair
lessons.check_note: Megillah 29a, Mishnah Gittin 4:2 and Etz Chaim 9:2 read on Sefaria 11/13. Broken-vessels summary and modern use of tikkun olam from memory (Scholem): check. Aleinu wording: CHECK Mishkan T'filah.

cards.title: God in exile
cards.body: Kabbalah speaks of the **Shechinah**, God's presence dwelling in the world, as close to us, and sometimes in exile with us.

cards.q: In the Talmud, the Divine Presence went into exile with Israel.
cards.why: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, in Megillah 29a.

cards.title: The Shechinah went with them
cards.body: **Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai**: see how beloved Israel is. Wherever they were exiled, **the Divine Presence went with them**: to Egypt, to Babylonia. And when they are redeemed, the Divine Presence will return **with them**.

cards.q: According to Megillah 29a, where was the Divine Presence when Israel was exiled?
cards.why: God **goes into exile** with the people.
wrong_why: The Talmud says the Presence went with them.

cards.title: Broken vessels
cards.body: Luria taught that the first vessels made to hold God's light **could not hold it**, and broke. Etz Chaim describes "seven kings" who descended, and from what was left of them the **klipot**, husks, were formed, with **lights** still caught inside. As scholars summarize it, every good act **frees a spark** and helps repair what broke.

src.ref: Etz Chaim 9:2 (Sefaria Community Translation); Gershom Scholem, Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism (1941)
src.note: from memory, not on Sefaria; check

cards.q: In Luria's picture, what is caught inside the husks (klipot)?
cards.why: **Sparks of light**, waiting to be raised.

src.ref: Etz Chaim 9:2 (Sefaria Community Translation); Gershom Scholem, Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism (1941)
src.note: from memory, not on Sefaria; check

cards.title: For the betterment of the world
cards.body: The phrase **tikkun olam** is old. In the Mishnah, **Rabban Gamliel the Elder** makes rules about divorce documents "for the betterment of the world": legal fixes that keep society **fair and working**.

cards.title: Tikkun olam today
cards.body: Many prayer books' **Aleinu** hopes to **repair the world** under God's sovereignty. Kabbalah gave the idea a cosmic meaning, and modern Reform Judaism made **tikkun olam** a call to **social justice**: repair, one act at a time.

src.ref: Aleinu (second paragraph); Reform usage of tikkun olam
src.note: CHECK: Mishkan T'filah Aleinu wording; history from memory

cards.q: In the Mishnah, what does "for the betterment of the world" refer to?
choices: Practical rules that keep society fair
cards.why: Tikkun olam begins as **law** for a fair society.
wrong_why: That meaning comes later, from Kabbalah.

cards.prompt: Luria pictures a broken world with light hidden in every piece. Where have you found light inside something broken?

points: Megillah 29a: **the Shechinah goes into exile** with Israel.
Luria: **vessels broke**; sparks are caught in husks.
Mishnah Gittin: tikkun olam as **fair law**.
Today: **repair**, one act at a time.
